payload.finalHint: Each one fixes a single named note to a single line of the staff

explanations: The treble clef is the G-clef in its usual position, placing G above middle C on the second line of the staff.
The bass clef is the F-clef, fixing the F below middle C on the fourth line; Good Boys Do Fine Always names its lines.
The alto clef is the C-clef in its commonest position, placing middle C on the third line, and is used for middle parts.
Treble, bass and alto are three clefs: symbols that fix one named note to one line, so the rest of the staff can be read.

sources.excerpt: In modern music notation, the G-clef is most frequently seen as treble clef (placing G4 on the second line of the staff), and the F-clef as bass clef (placing F3 on the fourth line).
For example, even the low saxophones read in treble clef.
Placing these clefs on a line fixes a reference note to that line—an F-clef fixes the F below middle C, a C-clef fixes middle C, and a G-clef fixes the G above middle C.
The C-clef is mostly encountered as alto clef (placing middle C on the third line) or tenor clef (middle C on the fourth line).
To this end, the G-clef is used for high parts, the C-clef for middle parts, and the F-clef for low parts.
A clef (from French: clef 'key') is a musical symbol used to indicate which notes are represented by the lines and spaces on a musical staff.
